location: The PID lecture: not chosen yet. Lucky picks the lecture and checks each key claim against it (docs/lesson-drone-pid.md, reading guide).

key_claims: A feedback controller measures, compares with the target, and corrects, over and over.
P pushes in proportion to the current gap.
With gravity, P alone leaves the drone below the target, because it needs a gap to make the thrust that holds it up.
D pushes against the speed of change, which damps the bounce. At rest it adds nothing.
I adds up the gap over time, so it keeps increasing thrust until the gap is zero. At rest it holds the weight.
Too much P or I causes overshoot and ringing (too much I can stop it settling at all); too much D makes it sluggish, and on real drones amplifies sensor noise.
misconceptions: "D makes the drone go faster." It does the opposite: it resists fast changes.
"I is just a stronger P." P reacts to the gap now; I reacts to the gap's history.
"Bigger gains are always better." They trade a smaller gap for more bounce, and motors have a limit.
"The controller knows the drone's weight." A basic PID doesn't; it only sees the gap.
"P only should reach the target eventually if you wait." With a constant pull like gravity, it never does.
teach_back_prompts: In one sentence each, what do P, I and D do?
Why does a P-only drone hover low?
guide.application_question: A delivery drone picks up a parcel mid-flight. What happens to its height with P and D only, and what fixes it?
